newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Geography makes Russian oil firm integration tough.
newsitem.headline: Geography makes Russian oil firm integration tough.

text.p: A push by Russian oil companies to tighten integration of their upstream and downstream operations is unlikely to lead to major changes in their mix of oil products, energy analysts said on Tuesday.
But greater vertical integration could help secure crude deliveries to some refineries and improve the running of downstream operations, they said.

"Most of the vertically-integrated oil companies are starting to try to exert more control over what is happening," said Peter Houlder, energy analyst and managing director at CentreInvest in Moscow. "It should have some beneficial effects."

Tyumen Oil Company, ranking fifth in Russia's production league, is the latest firm vying to tighten its grip over subsidiaries, announcing on Monday that it intended to take over full managerial control of its troubled Ryazan refinery.
Similar steps have been taken by other Russian majors like LUKoil, the country's biggest, YUKOS and SIDANKO.

Tyumen Oil also said it would transfer 30 percent of shares in Nizhnevartovskneftegaz, its main producing unit, to the Ryazan refinery. Analysts said such transfers appeared to be targeted at securing crude supplies to refineries.
"Companies feel a lot safer being the masters of their own supplies," said Michael Sausman, vice-president of Arthur D. Little consultants in Moscow.

Integration in Russia's oil sector, begun several years ago to turn the old production associations into corporate entities, has forced the world's newest majors to face the fact that their refining and production bases are separated by vast distances.

Sausman said the huge distances separating upstream and downstream operations meant Russian refineries often had to buy oil from outsiders for processing, limiting the extent to which companies could become fully integrated entities.
"This is all mainly because of locational questions. (Russian) oil is not necessarily transportable in an economic way," he said.
Refineries often operate under tolling deals, whereby they are paid to process oil from other companies which are better geographically situated to supply raw materials.
The Ryazan plant, for example, lies about 2,000 km (1,240 miles) west of Tyumen Oil's main output unit in Western Siberia.
Output at Russia's seventh largest refinery is running at just 23 percent nameplate capacity, slumping to 82,600 bpd in 1996 from 148,300 bpd in 1995.

In theory, fuller vertical integration would give Russian oil firms greater flexibility in the mix of crude oil and oil products they produce and export, offering some protection against fluctuations in world oil and product prices.

But factors special to the world's third biggest oil producer after Saudi Arabia and the United States suggest that Russia's aggressive crude oil exporting will continue for some time to come, analysts said.

Russia refined 3.52 million bpd of oil in 1996, down three percent from 1995, and only 50-60 percent of its full processing capacity. Oil production slipped as well, but exports of crude last year jumped nine percent to 2.1 million bpd.
Domestic demand for oil products was unlikely to pick up significantly this year, despite signs that Russian's ailing economy was at long last starting to stabilise.
"At the end of the day, refineries can't sell any more than the public wants to buy," Sausman said.
Opportunities for boosting oil product exports also looked bleak, given that Western Europe, as well as Russia, already faces refining overcapacity.
"Given the overall level of demand for products, there is at least one, may be two completely surplus (Russian) refineries, and this is a European-wide phenomenon," Houlder said.

Most Russian refineries lack the technology to produce larger amounts of high-value products like gasoline and jet fuel, and so churn out large volumes of cheaper products like heavy fuel oil instead.
Heavy fuel oil accounted for 36 percent of 1996 refining output, while higher-valued gasoline accounted for 15 percent.
